671.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, that which you have to do tomorrow - do it today instead; and that which you have to do now - do it immediately! Later on, you will not be able to do anything, when death hangs over your head.”
671.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, whose saloks the Gurus included in the scripture, warns that putting off what has been resolved is fatal, because the time to act can close without warning.
671.tie_back: The Kural says that once a decision is reached, letting it sink into delay is a positive harm; Kabir likewise treats postponement of a settled duty as the real danger.
671.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Kabir (Salok 138), Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
671._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the evil of delaying what must be done, though Kabir's context is spiritual (remembrance of God before death) rather than executing a ruler's counsel.

672.quote_or_event: “In all ten directions, the branches are green and alive. That which ripens slowly, is sweet.”
672.explanation: In his Baarah Maahaa (song of the twelve months) Guru Nanak observes that fruit which ripens in its own time is the sweet one, an image of patient, unhurried growth toward the Beloved.
672.tie_back: The Kural's first half says some tasks are properly done slowly; Guru Nanak's image of slow ripening honours exactly that kind of patience, while Kabir's call to act at once (see Kural 671) matches the second half.
672.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1109, Raag Tukhaari, Baarah Maahaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
672._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the line supports only the 'take your time' half of the couplet, and its setting is the soul's spiritual ripening, not the timing of practical undertakings.

673.quote_or_event: In the Zafarnama, the Persian letter Guru Gobind Singh sent to the emperor Aurangzeb in 1705, verse 22 states the principle that when every other means of redressing a wrong has failed, it is lawful and just to take up the sword.
673.explanation: The verse, borrowed almost word for word from Saadi, became a classic summary of the Sikh idea of righteous struggle (dharam yudh): force is legitimate only after other means have been tried and have failed.
673.tie_back: The Kural teaches choosing the means that will actually work, direct action where possible and another route where not; the Zafarnama also grades the means, but in the reverse order, putting force last.
673.source: Guru Gobind Singh, Zafarnama, verse 22 (Dasam Granth), as summarised in Wikipedia, Zafarnama (letter)
673._accuracy_note: Next-best only: nothing in the Guru Granth Sahib fits this strategic maxim, so this uses the Dasam Granth (whose authorship is contested within Sikhism) via Wikipedia as a last resort, and its order of means is the reverse of Parimelazhagar's reading.

674.quote_or_event: “If someone focuses on the Lord beforehand, then why should he be punished? The kings had lost their higher consciousness, reveling in pleasure and sensuality.”
674.explanation: Writing of Babur's invasion, Guru Nanak says the rulers who ignored the gathering danger while absorbed in pleasure were overtaken by disaster that foresight could have prevented.
674.tie_back: The Kural warns that a half-dealt-with enemy grows unnoticed like embers until it destroys the careless; Guru Nanak's lament shows rulers ruined by exactly such neglect of a danger they should have attended to in time.
674.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Ashtapadi (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
674._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shares the lesson that neglected danger destroys the negligent, but lacks the Kural's specific image of unfinished tasks and enemies regrowing like embers, and its main point is remembering God.

675.quote_or_event: “First, examine the merchandise, and then, make the deal.”
675.explanation: Guru Nanak uses the trader's rule of inspecting goods before buying as a model for judging carefully before committing oneself.
675.tie_back: The Kural tells one to think through resources, means, time, the act and place until no doubt remains before acting; Guru Nanak's saying states the same principle of full appraisal before commitment.
675.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1410, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
675._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on examining before acting, though it gives no five-part checklist and is used in Gurbani for spiritual discernment.

676.quote_or_event: “So throw the dice in such a way, that you shall not lose with your Lord and Master. Do those deeds which shall bring you profit.”
676.explanation: In Asa ki Vaar Guru Nanak uses the image of a calculated move in a game, urging that one's efforts be chosen so that they end in gain rather than loss before the Lord.
676.tie_back: The Kural asks one to weigh the effort, the obstacles and the great gain of a task before acting; Guru Nanak likewise asks for deeds weighed by their final profit.
676.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa ki Vaar (Pauri 21), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
676._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: shares the cost-and-gain reckoning, but the profit meant is spiritual standing with God, and the separate weighing of obstacles is absent.

677.quote_or_event: “Go and ask the happy, pure soul-brides, how did they obtain their Husband Lord?”
677.explanation: Guru Nanak tells the seeker to learn the way from those who have already reached the goal, rather than relying on cleverness of one's own.
677.tie_back: The Kural says the right method is to take the mind of one who knows the task from the inside, having done it before; Guru Nanak sends the seeker to those who have already succeeded.
677.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 722, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
677._accuracy_note: Strong structural fit (learn from the experienced), though the 'task' in Gurbani is union with the Divine and the bride-soul image is spiritual, not practical.

678.quote_or_event: “Servant Nanak begs for the dust of the feet of that GurSikh, who himself chants the Naam, and inspires others to chant it.”
678.explanation: Guru Ram Das honours the Sikh whose own practice becomes the means of drawing others into the same practice.
678.tie_back: The Kural pictures one achievement used to secure another, like a tamed elephant luring a wild one; the Gurbani image is of one who, having made the Name his own, draws others to it.
678.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 306, Raag Gauree, Gauri ki Vaar (salok), Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
678._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Sikh scripture has no teaching on using one undertaking to accomplish the next; this offers only a loose analogy of one success drawing in others.

679.quote_or_event: “No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone.”
679.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the state reached in the company of the holy, in which enmity and estrangement fall away altogether.
679.tie_back: The Kural ranks winning over those not yet on one's side above favouring existing friends; Guru Arjan goes further, dissolving the line between friend and foe entirely.
679.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
679._accuracy_note: Partial: shares the move from enmity to concord, but the Kural's advice is strategic alliance-building, while Guru Arjan describes an inner spiritual state.

680.quote_or_event: “When something is placed on the balancing scale and weighed, the side which descends is heavier.”
680.explanation: In Asa ki Vaar Guru Nanak uses the scale to show that the one who bows is the one of real weight, so humility is strength, not loss.
680.tie_back: The Kural says the rulers of a small realm, fearing for their people, will bow to a greater power when peace is offered; Guru Nanak's scale gives a moral reason why such bowing need not be shameful.
680.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa, Asa ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
680._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Guru Nanak praises humility as a virtue before God and others, not political submission by a weaker state to a stronger one.
